newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon remains good fit for Hughes.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon remains good fit for Hughes.

text.p: Raytheon Co's proposed acquisition of Texas Instruments Inc's defense assets does not make the company any more attractive as a partner for Hughes Electronics Corp, but the two would still fit well together, analysts said on Monday.
"Hughes would fit the best with Raytheon now without a doubt," said Jack Modzelewski, an analyst with PaineWebber.

Analysts said Raytheon and Hughes, a unit of General Motors Corp, have many overlapping strengths and their union would create a missile powerhouse. But any deal could hinge on whether GM prefered an all-cash sale or a transaction that had a stock component.
Raytheon would emerge as the strongest bidder if General Motors Corp sought equity in the acquiring company in exchange for its stake, analysts said.
If GM wanted a cash deal, Northrop Grumman Corp -- also thought to be a Hughes suitor -- would be an equally strong bidder, said analyst Cai Von Rumohr of Cowen & Co.
Modzelewski said GM would probably sell Hughes for equity because of tax and accounting reasons. Hughes is thought to be worth around $9 billion.
"I think ultimately (Raytheon) will try to put a bid in for Hughes. They'll probably try to do that with stock," he said.
Still, Northrup could offer a higher amount of cash -- as Raytheon did Monday with its takeover of Texas Instruments' defense assets -- to offset the tax consequences, analysts said.

Even so, Peter Aseritis, an analyst with CS First Boston, said Raytheon would not necessarily be the favored bidder. "I don't think making (the Texas Instruments) acquisition hurts them, but I don't think it will give them any leg up," he said.
To be sure, the recent merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp may force Lockheed Martin Corp into the bidding for Hughes, Aseritis said.
But both Modzelewski and Von Rumohr said antitrust issues would probably keep Lockheed and Hughes from joining forces.
The Wall Street Journal reported that final bids for Hughes were due on Monday, although Hughes officials declined to comment on a date.

A deal with Hughes would likely spur Raytheon to spin off its $3 billion engineering and construction business and sell its $2 billion appliance divison to concentrate on again becoming a defense business, Modzelewski said.
While a merger between Raytheon and Hughes would join together two companies that were often direct competitors, there was little overlap in the Texas Instruments deal, analysts said.
All three analysts said the $2.95 billion price for Texas Instruments' defense operations, to be renamed Raytheon TI Systems, was high, even with a $550 million tax credit for goodwill from the deal.
"It's a full price. Even $2.4 billion probably still sets the high-water mark," Modzelewski said.
Aseritis, who has a hold recommendation on Raytheon, and Modzelewski, who has an 'accumulate' rating, both said the deal will have no impact on their earnings outlook for Raytheon for 1996 or 1997.
